summary: Joseph's steward finds the planted cup in Benjamin's sack, and all the brothers return to face judgment. Judah offers to remain enslaved in Benjamin's place to spare their father, prompting Joseph to reveal himself and summon the family to Egypt; Jacob's disbelief gives way to renewed hope when he sees the wagons.
whyItMatters: Judah's willingness to bear Benjamin's fate shows the family loyalty Joseph was testing. Reconciliation then becomes a practical rescue from the remaining years of famine.

context.author: In the book's Sinai frame an angel recounts this material to Moses. That narrative speaker is distinct from the historical author, whom this chapter does not identify.
context.audience: Moses receives the account inside the story for Israel and its descendants. The historical work addresses Jewish concerns about covenant, inherited stories, and observance; a specific first community is uncertain.
context.date: The narrative uses a chronology counted from creation within its Sinai revelation frame. The historical work is usually placed in the second century BCE; an exact composition date is not established.
context.setting: The road out of Egypt, Joseph's house and judgment setting, and Jacob's home where the brothers report Joseph alive.
context.literaryForm: Test and recognition narrative with an intercessory speech, emotional revelation, and preparations for migration.

before.text: Joseph has ordered the silver cup placed in Benjamin's sack in order to learn whether the brothers now intend peace toward one another.

here.text: The decisive moment is Judah's offer to take Benjamin's place, after which Joseph recognizes their solidarity and ends the deception.

after.text: Jacob pauses on the journey to seek assurance about leaving the land and receives a promise of God's presence in Egypt.

outline.heading: The staged accusation and search
outline.note: The steward pursues, rejects the brothers’ proposed death penalty, and finds the planted cup.

outline.heading: The brothers return together
outline.note: All come back, but Joseph offers to retain only Benjamin as a servant.

outline.heading: Judah offers himself
outline.note: He explains the danger to their father and asks to remain instead of Benjamin.

outline.heading: Joseph reveals himself and calls for the family
outline.note: He recognizes their unity, weeps, identifies himself, and interprets his role as preserving life.

outline.heading: Supplies and Jacob’s revived hope
outline.note: Pharaoh authorizes transport and provisions; the wagons help Jacob believe the news.

keyVerses.text: Now rather let me, thy servant, abide instead of the boy as a bondsman unto my lord, and let the lad go with his brethren, for I became surety for him at the hand of thy servant our father, and if I do not bring him back, thy servant will hear the blame to our father for ever.'
keyVerses.why: Judah’s willingness to become a bondsman in Benjamin’s place provides the concrete proof of responsibility.

keyVerses.text: Come down quickly ye and your households, so that ye perish not through the famine, and do not be grieved for your possessions, for the Lord sent me before you to set things in order that many people might live.
keyVerses.why: Joseph interprets his presence in Egypt as preparation for preserving many lives.

keyVerses.text: And their father did not believe it, for he was beside himself in his mind; but when he saw the wagons which Joseph had sent, the life of his spirit revived, and he said: 'It is enough for me if Joseph lives; I will go down and see him before I die.'
keyVerses.why: The wagons make the improbable report credible enough for Jacob to resolve to travel.

questions.question: Is Benjamin guilty of stealing the cup?
questions.answer: No. The reader is told that the steward places it in his sack at Joseph's command. The accusation is staged, so the cup's discovery proves possession created by the test rather than an actual theft.

questions.question: Do the brothers abandon Benjamin when the cup is found?
questions.answer: They tear their clothes in grief and all return to Joseph. Joseph offers to let the others leave, but Judah's speech refuses to save himself at Benjamin's expense.

questions.question: What does Judah mean by being a “surety”?
questions.answer: He has taken personal responsibility to his father for bringing Benjamin home. His offer to remain as a bondsman turns that promise into a willingness to bear Benjamin's threatened fate himself.

questions.question: Why is Jacob’s likely grief central to Judah’s appeal?
questions.answer: Judah explains that their father believes one of Rachel's sons lost and has bound his life to the remaining son. Leaving Benjamin behind would therefore mean returning with news Judah believes would kill their father.

questions.question: What causes Joseph to reveal himself?
questions.answer: The narrator says he sees that all the brothers are united in goodness toward one another. His inability to restrain himself follows Judah's offer, connecting recognition of changed relations with disclosure of his identity.

questions.question: Does Joseph’s claim of divine purpose excuse the original harm?
questions.answer: Joseph says God sent him ahead so that many could live through the famine. That is his interpretation of how rescue has emerged from events; the passage does not say the earlier betrayal was morally right or make deliberate harm a method to imitate.

questions.question: Why does Jacob believe after seeing the wagons?
questions.answer: He initially cannot accept the report that Joseph is alive and rules Egypt. The visible transport Joseph sends revives his spirit and enables him to commit to the journey, though the chapter does not describe every step of that recognition.

glossary.def: A person who undertakes responsibility for another’s safe return, as Judah has done for Benjamin.
A person held in service or slavery, the status Judah offers to accept instead of Benjamin.
Repaid or returned; the steward’s accusation claims the brothers have answered kindness with wrongdoing.
